newsitem.title: USA: Clinton given chance to stack Fed with Democrats. [CORRECTED 09:20 GMT 11/1]
newsitem.headline: Clinton given chance to stack Fed with Democrats. [CORRECTED 09:20 GMT 11/1]

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
President Clinton was handed the opportunity to stack the board of the powerful Federal Reserve with Democrats Friday, after Republican Lawrence Lindsey said he will step down.

But analysts said it was not clear how much difference that would make, especially as regards interest rate policy, given the pre-eminence of Chairman Alan Greenspan, a Republican, whose policy has been surprisingly in synch with Clinton.
"(Greenspan) is so firmly in control that it is hard to conceive of much of a challenge to his authority," said David Jones, vice chairman of Wall Street brokerage Aubrey G. Lanston and Co.
Lindsey is leaving the central bank after five years as a governor to join the conservative American Enterprise Institute.
His departure leaves two vacancies on the seven-member board. Janet Yellen, who was named by Clinton to the Fed 2-1/2 years ago, is leaving to become chief White House economist.
Two Clinton nominees are already serving on the Fed board -- Vice Chairwoman Alice Rivlin and Gov. Laurence Meyer.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the administration was in the early stages of looking for replacements for Yellen and Lindsey and was unlikely to have any nominees before the Fed's next policy-making meeting on Feb. 4-5.
"We're very early in the process and it's hard to imagine, given where we are in the process, that we would have nominees in place in time for that meeting," McCurry told reporters.
Administration officials said they expect Clinton to try to fill at least one of the Fed positions with a woman or a member of a minority group. But no specific names were mentioned.

Among those cited in the past have been former Atlanta Federal Reserve Bank economist Sheila Tschinkel (corrects to add word "former") and Northwestern University Professor Marcus Alexis, who is black.

Others that have been mentioned include professors Benjamin Friedman from Harvard and Peter Kenen from Princeton and bankers Anthony Terracciano, formerly of First Fidelity Bancorp., and John Medlin, who was with Wachovia Corp.
One official, who declined to be identified said he would not be surprised if Clinton came up with someone entirely new.
In the past, the administration has taken its time filling Fed governor posts, perhaps in part because of a perception among some policymakers of the dominance of the chairman.
Clinton last year reappointed Greenspan to a third term as head of the central bank.
Greenspan enjoys particularly cordial relations with Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin. The two meet regularly.
Contrary to his reputatation as a hard-nosed inflation fighter, Greenspan has, in the words of one Fed watcher, proven to be a "dove in hawk's clothing."
He successfully fought off pressure within the Fed for an interest rate increase last year ahead of the November presidential election.
Yellen, and to a lesser extent, Lindsey, also have reputations as being more dovish than hawkish on inflation.
That is one reason why some analysts do not expect Clinton's new nominees to make all that much difference in altering the central bank's interest rate policy.
Joel Prakken, Chairman of St. Louis-based Macroeconomic Advisers, said the two new Clinton appointees could serve as a counterweight to more hawkish regional bank presidents.

Two well-known inflation hawks, Al Broaddus of the Richmond Fed, and Robert Parry of San Francisco, became voting members this year of the central bank's Federal Open Market Committee, which sets interest rates.
Where the new appointements could make a difference, some analysts suggested, is in the regulatory arena, which is the province of the Fed board, rather then the FOMC.
Greenspan's predilection is to oppose increased regulation of the banking industry.
But Clinton's new appointees would presumably be less dogmatic in that regard and might even favour new measures to promote lending to the poor and minority groups, analysts said.
